newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-GREECE TO LOSE $14 MILLION FROM WORLD CHAMPS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-GREECE TO LOSE $14 MILLION FROM WORLD CHAMPS.

text.p: Athens will lose $14 million from organising the world athletics championship in August but officials promised success, a must for the city's bid to host the 2004 Olympic Games.

"I personally don't accept that the world championship is a prerequisite (for the Olympics) as often mentioned, but in any case it will be a success," Vangelis Savramis, the championship's general manager, told reporters late on Thursday.
Savramis said the financial loss would result from an unprofitable agreement between the International Amateur Athletics Federation (IAAF) and the Greek Athletics Federation (SEGAS).
He said SEGAS did not seek any financial help from IAAF when it asked to host the championship in 1995 after Mexico City, which was offered by IAAF $4 million, rejected the championship.

Savramis said SEGAS offered generous accomodation and leisure packages to hundreds of IAAF officials and submitted a false budget which called for a $8.75 million revenue from ticket sales and $8.52 million in expenses.

"The agreement with IAAF was signed jointly by SEGAS, the sports ministry, former Prime Minister Andreas Papandreou, the Athens municipality and the state television," SEGAS President Stratos Molivas toild Reuters.
"Mr Savramis is an employee of the state (sports ministry) and he does not represent anybody. We've prepared a protest letter to the sports ministry," he added.

Savramis' and Molivas' comments were in the context of a year-long stubborn power game between the Greek sports ministry and SEGAS on who has the upper hand to organise the event, prompting IAAF to sent several warnings to both bodies.
"If Greece is bidding for the 2004 Olympics and it can't organise the world championship then this bid must be withdrawn," IAAF President Primo Nebiolo said during a recent visit to Athens.

"The world championship is the greatest sports event of 1997. We will have the best athletes and thousands of journalists. Greece is lucky to have this event and if the Greeks are united they will have no problems," he added.
SEGAS briefly withdrew from the championship's organising committee last October, saying it was being marginalised by the state.
"I can say that all of us try to destroy this championship which for good or bad came to Greece," Savramis said.

But he stressed that the championship would be a big success with state-of-the-art television coverage and telecommunications along with strict security measures and proper accomodation for athletes, the press and IAAF officials.
The championship is seen as a major test for Athens' bid to host the 2004 Olympic Games and it will be held one month before the International Olympic Committee announces the host city.

Athens lost last year's Games to Atlanta for its lack of organisation and poor infrastructure and had threatened to boycott centennial Olympic festivities in Atlanta and never bid for the Games again.
But it has put together a better bidding dossier for the 2004 Games and is considered among the favourites along with Rome, Cape town and Stockholm.
